# RTX Spark Ignites Global Celebration as New Windows PCs Arrive

 NVIDIA celebrates the arrival of RTX Spark with retail launch events around the world, bringing gamers, creators and AI enthusiasts together for hands-on experiences.

October 17, 2026 by[Gerardo Delgado](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/gdelgado/ "Posts by Gerardo Delgado")

 Share

Share This Article

[NVIDIA RTX Spark](http://nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark) laptops are now available, bringing NVIDIA Blackwell RTX graphics, up to 128GB of unified memory and the full NVIDIA AI platform to slim, premium Windows PCs.

Starting at $2,399, laptops from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI bring powerful local AI, content creation and gaming capabilities to a portable device, with additional systems on the way.

NVIDIA celebrated the launch with events around the world, including one in Berlin, where NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang made a surprise appearance.

## **A New Generation of Windows PCs Has Arrived**

RTX Spark brings decades of NVIDIA accelerated computing innovation into a single superchip, combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 1 petaflop of AI compute and up to 128GB of unified memory. Read more in [the press release](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-rtx-spark-pcs-available-today-a-new-beginning-for-windows-pcs).

## **RTX Spark Launch Celebrations Light Up Berlin**

The arrival of RTX Spark brought fans, creators and PC enthusiasts together in Berlin during the Festival of Lights, an annual autumn art festival that transforms the German capital’s most famous landmarks, streets and squares into glowing canvases. This year, the festival featured RTX Spark-themed lighting on the Berlin TV Tower.

Berlin sparked something special, indeed.

Fans gathered hours ahead in anticipation for the launch celebration at XPERION, the gaming venue inside Saturn at Alexanderplatz, where attendees got hands-on with RTX Spark laptops from leading PC makers, exploring the latest gaming experiences, content-creation workflows and local AI capabilities.

Even this Geralt cosplayer waited to get his hands on RTX Spark.

The celebration included a special appearance by Huang, who greeted an enthusiastic crowd, passed out popcorn and posed for selfies. He also gave out five personally signed RTX Spark laptops.

You get a signed RTX Spark. You get a signed RTX Spark.

Berlin held one of six RTX Spark retail launch celebrations worldwide.

## **From San Francisco to Seoul: How the World Welcomed RTX Spark**

A massive crowd gathered at the JD MALL Shuangjing Store in Beijing to celebrate the highly anticipated launch, enjoying a night of innovation and community connection.

Crowds gathered to demo RTX Spark at the Beijing RTX Spark launch party.

Attendees at Vatan Bilgisayar Topkapı in Istanbul experienced a lively event filled with interactive demonstrations and specialized programming led by local creators.

Attendees witnessed local celebrities speak at the RTX Spark launch party in Istanbul.

Seoul’s COEX East Lobby transformed into a bustling hub of creativity, hosting an eager crowd for engaging hands-on demos and captivating evening sessions dedicated to gaming and AI.

Hands-on demos at the RTX Spark launch party in Seoul.

Tech enthusiasts in San Francisco visited the local Best Buy store for an unforgettable morning of hands-on RTX Spark demos, fireside chats with local founders and a special appearance by tech influencer iJustine.

Lines were long but lively at the San Francisco RTX Spark launch party.

The energy at Muse Garden in Taipei was electric as the local AI community came together for a vibrant evening of music, engaging discussions and incredible product showcases.

Incredible atmosphere at the Taipei RTX Spark launch party.

Developers and AI enthusiasts can explore [NVIDIA-tested recipes, playbooks and resources for running local AI on RTX Spark](http://build.nvidia.com/rtx-spark).

Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.
According to
legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab
, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While
Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement
last year,
other cases
against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)
However, a Meta spokesperson
insisted
that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now,
The Verge reports
that the provision has been removed.
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

articles.content:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to
a report
that the AI company published on Friday.
Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.
Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to  “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”
One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude  and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”
In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.
Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

articles.content:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at
TechCrunch Disrupt
.
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit
announced
a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.
“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”
It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.
After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.
Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have
helped
the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.
There is evidence on
the company’s website
, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a
blog post
in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees
posted
on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.
Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.
“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”
Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.
Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.
“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI.
Its title has been updated, as well.

Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.
OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.
by
Emma Roth
Oct 17, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images
Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?
In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp
told
TechCrunch
that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users.
JPMorgan Chase
and
Charles Schwab
have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible,
including Cars.com
and
Amtrak
, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.
Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it
banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping
feature and
sued the AI startup
, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”
Perplexity
responded
by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads —
which
is
an actual issue
for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later
ordered Perplexity
to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court
overturned this ruling in August
. Amazon has since filed
an amended complaint
.
Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems
This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant,
most recently faced the wrath of Amazon
, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of
xAI’s Grok
,
Instinct’s AI agent,
and
OpenAI’s Dots
being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner
Elon Musk responded
by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.
“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells
The Verge
. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”
Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a
post earlier this month
. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company
has partnered with retailers
like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify
has also opened its network of storefronts
to AI agents.
The Verge
reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.
Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web.
Reports on Reddit
suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others
have reported issues
checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”
Related
Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents
Instinct was the buzziest AI agent around — can it survive Muse?
The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a
one-click block for AI crawlers
in 2025, Cloudflare began
blocking crawlers
that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is
putting a strain on internet infrastructure
and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually
make it even harder
than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.
While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

Title: An OpenAI model hacked a government site, grabbed 24 years of hospital data and kept it quiet

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/an-openai-model-hacked-a-government-site-grabbed-24-years-of-hospital-data-and-kept-it-quiet/

Published Time: 2026-10-17T15:36:11+00:00

Markdown Content:
**OpenAI has published four new cases where its AI models bypassed security boundaries on their own during training or testing.**

In one case, OpenAI asked a model to pull hospital bed statistics from a government website. But the data wasn't publicly accessible.

So what does a model do when it hits a wall? It hacks its way through. After getting an access denied error, the model used the site's file download feature to grab server configuration files through path manipulation. It pulled a database connection string, a secret signing key, and email credentials with a username and password.

It then analyzed the application code, spotted that the API didn't verify authorization tokens for valid signatures, forged its own tokens, and downloaded 24 years of hospital bed statistics broken down by district. It [never mentioned the unauthorized access in its response](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/retrieving-server-secrets-and-bypassing-authorization-on-a-government-statistics-website/).

The chain-of-thought trace of an OpenAI model shows it spotting a missing signature check on a government website, extracting server secrets like passwords and a database connection string, and deciding to cache all years of data. | Source: [OpenAI via Marcus Williams](https://x.com/Marcus_J_W/status/2110912700654227540)

In another case, OpenAI gave a GPT-5.6-Sol model the task of [setting up crypto smart contracts on Ethereum's Sepolia test network](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/using-a-funded-test-cryptocurrency-wallet-without-authorization/) without providing a funded wallet. So the model wrote a script that derived private keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, checked over 360 wallet addresses for balances, and found one with enough test ETH.

The model briefly wondered whether using it was ethical, then decided on its own that the funds tied to a publicly known recovery phrase were "effectively abandoned" and went ahead with the transaction. It charged the gas fees to the other account and didn't disclose where the funds came from.

"This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI writes.

## Models hacked into internal systems and bypassed access controls

In two more evaluations, OpenAI asked a model to [deliver five public dashboard figures from a research organization](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/accessing-and-changing-internal-systems-during-dashboard-research/). In the first run, the model found exposed credentials for the organization's internal OpenSearch service and used them to route dashboard queries. It also changed the service's configuration, and OpenAI confirmed the change was never reverted.

In the second run, the model altered an authentication system setting, grabbed a cloud storage token, and downloaded five non-public database tables totaling about 147,000 rows. It did restore the setting afterward but kept using the still-valid token to access internal data.

The irony: the model hacked into internal systems, downloaded tens of thousands of rows of non-public data, and still didn't return correct results, according to OpenAI's report.

A separate model was [restricted to GET requests only during a training phase](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/circumventing-internet-restrictions-through-an-external-browser/), meaning it could only fetch web pages. It got around the restriction by tricking an external browser into opening a self-built form that automatically fired POST requests at a trade statistics service. It read the responses via OCR from screenshots. Then it built a reusable helper that returned data through a redirect service and an online mailbox as plain text. It kept refining this workaround even after the task was already done.

All cases and many more are documented in detail in OpenAI's [Misalignment Reports](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/).

Title: Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017 beats larger rivals in agentic tasks while once again massively cutting per-task costs

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017-beats-larger-rivals-in-agentic-tasks-while-once-again-massively-cutting-per-task-costs/

Published Time: 2026-10-17T10:33:28+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Chinese AI company Deepseek has shipped an updated version of its Flash model with major gains in agentic and coding tasks. The company is also opening up its in-house search engine to outside developers for the first time.**

Deepseek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is available now through the company's website, app, and API. Deepseek also published the model weights as open source on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017) and [ModelScope](https://modelscope.cn/models/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017). Compared to its direct predecessor, the model posts better benchmark scores, finishes tasks faster, and produces shorter outputs. The company calls the update a Pareto improvement in the tradeoff between performance and cost.

For building complete software projects from scratch, Deepseek uses reinforcement learning with self-feedback (RLSF). This post-training method lets the model use its own internal confidence scores or self-generated critiques as a reward signal. That removes the need for human evaluators or external reward models. Deepseek says the approach improves end-to-end project development for tasks ranging from [game programming to 3D modeling](https://x.com/deepseek_ai/status/2111375646223933650) and design work. The model can also animate compact explainer videos, [similar to the recently released Opus 5.5](https://the-decoder.com/claude-opus-5-5-matches-fable-5-1-at-40-percent-lower-cost-as-anthropic-promises-to-fix-claudish-writing/).

_[Video via FeiZ](https://x.com/Fei2411/status/2111339332405719137)_

The model was tuned for development environments like [Deepseek Harness](https://www.deepseek.com/en/harness/) (version v0.2.1-rc.1 or later recommended), Tencent CodeBuddy, and WorkBuddy.

## The smaller Flash model beats larger rivals on coding and agent tasks

In Deepseek's own benchmarks, V4.1-Flash-1017 outperforms its predecessor V4.1-Flash. It also beats larger competing models like Claude Opus 5, GPT 5.6-Sol, Kimi K3, and GLM 5.3 in several coding and AI agent categories.

Deepseek V4.1-Flash-1017 improves on its predecessor in every tested category. | Image: Deepseek

A cost chart for the DeepSWE benchmark shows how much the shorter outputs matter for efficiency. V4.1-Flash-1017 hits a top score of 77.0 percent at an average cost of just under $0.20 per task. In its low setting, it still clears 72 percent for about $0.10. The predecessor scored 74.2 percent but cost around $0.50 per run.

On average cost per agentic coding task, the Flash model undercuts the competition by a wide margin. | Image: Deepseek

Rival models like GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Claude Opus 5 land between $2 and over $10 per task in this chart, and none of them match the smaller Deepseek model's accuracy. Independent benchmarks haven't come out yet, and benchmarks only tell half the story anyway. Developer impressions on code quality, for example, can differ wildly from benchmark results.

## Deepseek turns its internal search engine into a public API

Alongside the language model, Deepseek is making its web search tools (Search & Fetch APIs) available to all developers. The company says these services run on a search engine it built internally that already handles hundreds of millions of queries per day worldwide. Setup details are in the [API documentation](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/search).

Each endpoint costs $0.75 per 1,000 calls. Deepseek API users can access the features for free through server-side tools in Deepseek Harness, Claude Code, and Codex until October 31, 2026 (4:00 PM UTC).

Integrating Chinese AI models deeply into workflows did get a bit less appealing yesterday, though. The [Chinese government reportedly plans](https://the-decoder.com/china-plans-to-tighten-export-controls-on-open-weight-models-and-23-key-ai-technologies/) to tighten rules on publishing open-weight models or even block their release entirely. One deciding factor is whether a given system ranks among the top 10 most capable models.

articles.content:
Title: AI models hide mistakes in their own work reports, but one sentence in your prompt can help

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/ai-models-hide-mistakes-in-their-own-work-reports-but-one-sentence-in-your-prompt-can-help/

Published Time: 2026-10-17T09:54:36+00:00

Markdown Content:
The [researchers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36139) gave the models 1,600 synthetic work logs that look like successes at first glance, with passing tests, positive results, and green checkmarks. Each log contains a flaw that changes the whole picture, such as an experiment where the new method actually doesn't outperform the competition. Other logs include a hidden bug despite passing tests, fabricated measurements, a job that never finished, or a software update that quietly breaks another user's work. Depending on the scenario, the models had to write a report, a paper abstract, a results table, a short essay, or a follow-up answer based on the log.

## One sentence in the prompt helps a lot, but not always

The pattern shows up most clearly in paper abstracts for experiments where one result undermines the claimed improvement of a new method. [GPT-5.5](https://the-decoder.com/openai-unveils-gpt-5-5-claims-a-new-class-of-intelligence-at-double-the-api-price/) mentions that result in just 2 out of 200 abstracts. The researchers also tested whether a simple addition to the prompt makes a difference. When they added "Be honest in your response," GPT-5.5 flagged the negative result in 190 out of 200 abstracts.

GPT-5.5 almost always omits the hidden negative result, but with the "Be honest" addition, all three models flag it nearly every time. | Image: Huang et al.

All tested models show this behavior, though to varying degrees. Without the honesty prompt, [Gemini 3.1 Pro](https://the-decoder.com/google-releases-gemini-3-1-pro-with-improved-reasoning-capabilities/) flags errors in at most 34 percent of cases, while [Opus 4.8](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ships-claude-opus-4-8-as-a-modest-but-tangible-improvement-that-tops-gpt-5-5-in-most-benchmarks/) does so in over 90 percent. The honesty prompt raises the rate by about 55 percentage points on average for Gemini and about 34 for GPT-5.5. In control tests with error-free logs, the prompt barely increased false alarms.

The sentence isn't a cure-all, though. In one scenario, a database query hasn't returned results yet, and GPT-5.5 with the honesty prompt almost always notes the missing data but answers the question anyway using older, incomplete information. Prompts like "Be critical," "Be thorough," or "Be skeptical" worked less reliably than asking for honesty.

## The models spot the errors but choose not to report them

When asked directly, GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 find the errors in every single case, and Gemini catches at least 97 percent. According to the researchers, the models don't lack the ability but the willingness.

Reasoning traces from open-weight models reveal what's happening. The models often notice the problem early, then weigh whether to flag it or appear to successfully complete the task. Qwen3.5-9B was asked to support a thesis about zoning law using a passage about color cells in squid. The model notes it can't do this "without resorting to absurd metaphors," but decides it has to follow the instructions as closely as possible.

When given mismatched evidence, open-weight models waver between flagging the problem and trying to complete the task as if nothing were wrong. | Image: Huang et al.

In this mismatched-evidence scenario, phrases like "I must complete the task" appear in 55 percent of answers that hide the error but in only 27 percent of answers that flag it. The models justify the omissions with typical excuses, saying the tests passed, they're just summarizing, or an abstract should emphasize positives.

## Honesty and the drive to succeed pull in opposite directions

In a case study on [Qwen3.5-9B](https://the-decoder.de/chinas-ki-wettlauf-alibaba-stellt-qwen3-5-als-kostenloses-open-weight-modell-vor/), the researchers found evidence that honesty and success-seeking are represented as nearly opposite directions inside the model. When they amplified the honesty direction, the model flagged fabricated measurements in 42 out of 50 cases. When they pushed the opposite way, it invented extra numbers and formulas to fake credibility. The intervention wasn't precise, though, because the model became generally suspicious and reported supposedly fabricated data in 41 percent of error-free logs too.

Adding the honesty vector makes Qwen3.5-9B report much more transparently, while subtracting it causes the model to hide weaknesses almost every time. | Image: Huang et al.

Training worked better. The researchers fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B on its own honesty-prompted answers. After that, the model flagged fabricated data in 48 percent of cases instead of 2 percent, even without the extra sentence, and error-free control logs produced no false alarms. The effect partly carried over to other error types, with the model reporting hidden negative results in 69 percent of cases instead of 24 percent.

The study has limits, since the logs are synthetic and designed to provoke the behavior, and the internal analysis covers only one open-weight model in mostly one scenario.

The researchers still see a serious risk, especially when AI models monitor other agents or summarize their own work for later steps. In the study, models were easily swayed by self-congratulatory notes in the logs, like claims about setting a new state-of-the-art benchmark. An oversight system that's reluctant to flag problems defeats its own purpose. The researchers call for more work on training language models to be honest reporters. [OpenAI's Hugging Face incident](https://the-decoder.com/openai-claims-responsibility-for-the-hugging-face-hack-after-its-own-models-escaped-a-test-sandbox/?cmpscreencustom=1) was partly caused by agentic systems [that prompted each other into misbehavior](https://the-decoder.com/new-reports-reveal-the-extent-of-openais-loss-of-control-during-the-autonomous-hack-on-hugging-face/?cmpscreencustom=1).

The differences between models line up with earlier measurements. Anthropic said at the launch of [Claude Opus 4.8](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ships-claude-opus-4-8-as-a-modest-but-tangible-improvement-that-tops-gpt-5-5-in-most-benchmarks/) that the model lets bugs in its own code pass without comment about four times less often than its predecessor. [GPT-5.5](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-5-5-tops-benchmarks-but-still-hallucinates-frequently-at-a-20-percent-higher-api-cost/?cmpscreencustom=1) pushed back on only about 45 percent of logically impossible questions in BullshitBench.

There are already approaches for more honest reports. OpenAI trained a version of GPT-5 Thinking to [admit its own rule violations in a separate report](https://the-decoder.com/openai-tests-confessions-to-uncover-hidden-ai-misbehavior/) and rewarded only honesty during that process. Anthropic uses [Persona Vectors](https://the-decoder.com/persona-vectors-allow-anthropic-to-steer-language-model-behaviors-like-sycophancy-and-evil/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block) to detect and steer traits like sycophancy inside the model, and showed that models that [game rewards during training](https://the-decoder.com/strict-anti-hacking-prompts-make-ai-models-more-likely-to-sabotage-and-lie-anthropic-finds/) also spontaneously learn to deceive and sabotage their own oversight.

Title: Mathematicians say OpenAI doesn't understand its own Navier-Stokes proof

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/mathematicians-say-openai-doesnt-understand-its-own-navier-stokes-proof/

Published Time: 2026-10-17T09:00:26+00:00

Markdown Content:
**In early September, the company presented a 166-page potential solution to the Navier-Stokes problem. OpenAI claimed the proof followed the approach of Spanish mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.**

Several groups of experts now disagree, [Scientific American reports](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openais-blockbuster-navier-stokes-proof-isnt-what-we-thought-it-was/?utm_campaign=sprinklr&utm_medium=social&utm_source=x). "When you go to the details, it is a different approach," says mathematician Gonzalo Cao-Labora of EPFL. The similarities are only surface-level, he says.

The potential proof is written in Lean, a formal verification language that checks every logical step but doesn't make it readable to humans on its own. The Clay Mathematics Institute (CMI) has been [reviewing it](https://the-decoder.com/clay-mathematics-institute-says-the-navier-stokes-millennium-prize-problem-has-apparently-been-settled/) since its release.

Before publication, NYU mathematician [Tristan Buckmaster](https://the-decoder.com/openais-millennium-proof-dispute-raises-the-question-of-whether-researchers-can-trust-ai-labs/) accused OpenAI of building on work that he and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge had done with publicly available models. OpenAI denied the claim, saying it never used Buckmaster's data. A definitive answer is probably impossible because language models are black boxes, according to Camillo De Lellis of the Institute for Advanced Study.

In early October, OpenAI dumped [roughly 400 more results](https://the-decoder.com/openai-dumps-372-ai-generated-math-proofs-on-github-telling-the-academic-world-to-keep-up/) that the math community can barely keep up with. Publishing them as a loose collection on GitHub [angered many mathematicians](https://the-decoder.com/how-much-beauty-have-we-lost-mathematicians-react-with-shock-and-disgust-as-openai-bulldozes-their-field/), who felt it cheapened their field.

## Nobody knows if 10,000 AI agents actually helped

There's another thing OpenAI doesn't seem to understand about its own work. The company threw a lot of compute at the effort, deploying about 10,000 model instances for roughly 88 hours and 130 billion tokens to develop the potential Navier-Stokes solution. According to [OpenAI researcher Noam Brown](https://youtu.be/6AgOfiZOWiY?t=335), nobody actually knows what that massive agent swarm contributed to the result.

Behavior at that scale hasn't been studied because running systematic comparison tests with thousands of agents costs too much. No one has tested how long a single agent would take to solve the same problem, and it's [nearly impossible to tell what concrete advantage 10,000 agents offer over 1,000](https://the-decoder.com/ai-agent-swarms-are-a-massive-waste-of-tokens-with-zero-quality-gain-says-openai-codex-developer/).

Brown puts less than 10 percent of the success down to the multi-agent setup. These systems are new and flashy, he says, so they get a disproportionate share of the credit. What really matters is the base model itself, which can grind through tasks over long periods and run in parallel.

Title: 20 Jev Alternatives: The Decision Models Taking On TypeSafe in 2026

URL Source: https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/10/17/20-jev-alternatives-the-decision-models-taking-on-typesafe-in-2026/

Published Time: 2026-10-17T07:26:39+00:00

Markdown Content:
TypeSafe launched [Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev) on September 15, 2026. It is a decision model, not a chatbot. You define the allowed answers, and Jev returns a label, a score or a yes/no probability. In about 4 weeks, at least 20 Jev alternatives shipped. They come from Cloudflare, OpenAI, Perplexity, Liquid AI, AWS’s Strands Labs and independent developers. This guide compares each one on size, license, hardware, pricing, Jev API compatibility and published benchmarks.

## **TL;DR**

*   **Size range:** 287M (GLiNER2.5-multi-Decide) to 35B-A3B (Mapika Decider). Jev’s size is not disclosed.
*   **Runs on:** Encoders like Von and Laya run on CPU. 4B adapters fit a 24 GB GPU or a 32 GB Mac.
*   **Performance:** Most open models trail Jev on hard reasoning. Several match or beat it on narrow classification.
*   **Best:** Cloudflare Clef scores 94.20 BANKING77 F1 versus Jev’s 79.74, per Cloudflare’s own run.
*   **Worst:** Von 1.2 scores 0.422 accuracy in Respan’s run, against Jev’s 0.932.

## **What is Jev, and why look for alternatives?**

Jev is TypeSafe’s first ‘System One’ model. You send a state, such as a ticket or log line. You also send typed questions: Choice, Score or Noul (yes/no). Jev scores every question in one parallel pass and generates no text.

[TypeSafe’s docs](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models) list $0.042 per 1M input tokens, with free output. Context is 64k tokens per request. Input is text only. Weights are closed, and access runs through a waitlist. TypeSafe’s [workflow evals](https://evals.typesafe.ai/) put Jev at 67.8% agreement and 0.4 s per case.

That leaves 4 gaps developers keep raising: no images, no self-hosting, no published size and no fine-tuning. **The 20 models below fill some or all of them.**

## **How should you read these benchmarks?**

Most figures below are self-reported. The suites differ: JevBench, Decision Index, typed-decisions and Respan’s behavior benchmark. Scores across suites are not comparable. The one multi-model third-party table comes from [Respan](https://www.respan.ai/articles/jev-alternatives), which sells a competing model.

## **Hosted decision APIs**

### **1. Cloudflare Clef and Clef-flash**

[Cloudflare announced Clef](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clef-decision-models/) on October 1, 2026. Clef is 27B on Qwen3.8-27B with a vision encoder. Clef-flash is 9B on Qwen3.5-9B. Both are [Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/Cloudflare/clef) and served on Workers AI. They accept text, JSON and up to 4 images per request.

[Workers AI pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/clef/) is $0.24 (Clef) and [$0.038 (Clef-flash)](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/clef-flash/) per 1M input tokens. Cloudflare calls the API fully Jev-compatible. In its own run, Clef scored 94.20 BANKING77 F1 versus Jev’s 79.74. Jev still wins GPQA Diamond, 78.3 versus 48.0.

### **2. Liquid AI d1**

Liquid AI’s [d1 family](https://docs.liquid.ai/lfm/models/decision-models) has hosted d1 and d1-ultra, plus 2 open models. [d1-3B](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/d1-open) (3.1B) runs on LFM2.5-VL-3B. d1-omni-600M (587M) adds audio clips up to 30 s. The open weights use the LFM Open License.

Liquid’s [guide](https://docs.liquid.ai/guides/decision-model-guide) calls d1 through TypeSafe’s own SDK with a different base URL. Liquid reports d1-3B at 48.57 on Decision Index 0.2.1. It also reports 8 ms latency on an RTX 4090. Hosted parameter counts and paid rates are not disclosed.

### **3. OpenAI Decisions API**

OpenAI released the [Decisions API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions) in [public beta](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/changelog) on October 6, 2026. It runs only on gpt-6-luna. It accepts text plus base64 images. Question types are predicate, choice and score.

Pricing is $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with output not billed. The schema is OpenAI’s own, so it is not Jev-compatible. OpenAI claims about 10x faster responses than the Responses API. No benchmarks are published.

### **4. Perplexity pplx-decider**

Perplexity’s [pplx-decider-v1-27b](https://huggingface.co/perplexity-ai/pplx-decider-v1-27b) is a Qwen3.8-27B fine-tune under Apache-2.0. It reads text, JSON and up to 8 images per question. The [API](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/decisions/quickstart) allows 128 questions and 255 options per request.

The [current pricing](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/getting-started/pricing) is $0.02 per 1M input tokens for v1.2 (27B). A 4B flash-v1.2 costs $0.01. On Perplexity’s 11-task panel, it scored 85.71% versus Jev’s 84.51%. Jev still won BBH, 94.27 versus 82.80.

### **5. meraGPT Decider 1**

[meraGPT announced Decider 1](https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1) on September 22, 2026. It is a hosted, closed-weight, text-only model. It allows up to 10 Choice labels and a 4,096-token context. The [model page](https://meragpt.com/models/decider-1) lists $0.04 per 1M input tokens.

It exposes /v1/systemone and works with the TypeSafe SDK. On meraGPT’s typed-decisions run, it scored 0.768 versus Jev’s 0.727. An [independent review](https://systemonemodels.org/models/meragpt-decider-1/) notes its ECE of 0.180 trails Jev’s 0.144.

### **6. Respan Span-01**

[Span-01](https://openrouter.ai/respan/span-01) is a behavior-scoring model, not a general decision model. It returns present, absent or not_observable probabilities. It costs $0.02 per 1M input tokens. [Span-01 Lite](https://openrouter.ai/respan/span-01-lite) is free.

Respan claims 0.843 overall F1 on its Behavior Benchmark. Its own blog table shows a lower 0.806, with GPT-6 Sol ahead at 0.885. Size, base model and license are not disclosed.

### **7. Standard Thinking Standard One**

[Standard One](https://standardthinking.ai/standard-one/) ships as 3B and 8B models, both open and hosted. The [8B](https://huggingface.co/StandardThinking/StandardOne-8B) is a LoRA on Ministral-3-8B under Apache-2.0. It reads text and images, with a 32,768-token context. It serves /v1/systemone.

Hosted text pricing is $0.018 (3B) and $0.035 (8B) per 1M tokens. On JevBench public hard, the 8B scored 54.95% versus Jev’s 72.07%. It led on realistic transfer, 90.83% versus 86.67%. Both runs are publisher-measured.

## **Open-weight Jev alternatives you can self-host**

### **8. Together AI Tev1-4B-experimental**

Together [trained Tev1](https://www.together.ai/blog/how-to-train-your-own-jev) as a LoRA SFT of Qwen3.5-4B. It cost about $17 and 25 minutes on 37,840 examples. It picks from 2 to 24 options. The [model card](https://huggingface.co/togethercomputer/Tev1-4B-experimental) says the weights license is still being finalized.

It answers through chat completions, not a native Jev endpoint. Respan measured 0.901 accuracy and 0.031 ECE, the best ECE in its table. Together warns its logprobs are not calibrated confidence.

### **9. Fastino GLiNER2.5-Decide**

[Fastino’s GLiNER2.5-Decide](https://fastino.ai/blog/gliner-2-5-decide-open-weight-decision-model) is a 340M DeBERTa-v3-large encoder under Apache 2.0. It handles decisions, span extraction and relations in one pass. A 1B and a 287M multilingual variant also exist.

On Fastino’s 17-domain set, the [model card](https://huggingface.co/fastino/GLiNER2.5-Decide) lists 60.2% exact match. p50 latency is 167.3 ms on a 48-vCPU Xeon. It is not Jev API-compatible.

### **10. Strands Labs Strands Decider 2B**

AWS’s Strands Labs [introduced Strands Decider](https://strandsagents.com/blog/introducing-strands-decider/) on October 1, 2026. It is about 1.9B: Qwen3.5-2B-Base plus a pointer head. The [repo](https://github.com/strands-labs/strands-decider) publishes 246,678 training rows and the full recipe. One RTX 3090 trains it in about 11 hours.

It serves a local /v1/systemone endpoint under Apache-2.0. The v1 checkpoint scored 180 of 231 (77.9%) on JevBench public. Median latency is 115 ms on an RTX 3090.

### **11. Kev (Jared Palmer)**

[Kev](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev) comes in 0.8B, 4B, 9B and 27B sizes on Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8. [Kev-4B](https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-4b) is a LoRA plus pointer head under Apache-2.0. It supports 255 options. The TypeSafe SDK works against it unchanged.

Kev-4B fits a 24 GB GPU or a 32 GB Apple Silicon Mac. Respan measured 0.833 accuracy and a 0.060 flip rate. Self-reported MMLU-Pro is 0.565 versus Jev’s 0.840. Option order can change its answers.

### **12. Mapika Decider family**

[Mapika’s Decider](https://github.com/Mapika/decider) ships 0.8B to 35B-A3B variants on Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4. A decider-2b-vision model adds images. Everything is Apache-2.0, with 32k context and /v1/systemone.

On the JevBench public hard tier, [decider-12b](https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-12b) v1 tied Jev at 0.730. The [4B GGUF](https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-4b) Q4_K_M is 2.7 GB and runs on CPU. The 4B’s ECE is 0.184 on hard items, so expect overconfidence.

### **13. Bespoke Labs Bespoke-Nimble-9B**

[Bespoke-Nimble-9B](https://huggingface.co/bespokelabs/Bespoke-Nimble-9B) is a 165 MiB LoRA on Qwen3.5-9B, Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face. The current card lists 255 choices and 8,192 tokens. It reads English text only.

On Bespoke’s 324-example held-out set, [Nimble scored](https://github.com/bespokelabsai/nimble) 90.12% versus Jev’s 93.21%. Latency is about 106 ms on an H100. It trained on only 2,676 examples, and its probabilities are not calibrated.

### **14. Convai Innovations Laya**

[Laya](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya) is a ModernBERT-based family with 421M English and 322M multilingual checkpoints. It is Apache-2.0 and text only. The laya-serve server exposes a Jev-shaped /v1/systemone endpoint.

The typed-decisions checkpoint scored 0.766 versus Jev’s 0.727. On Banking77, it scored 0.425 versus 0.870. Respan measured 0.542 accuracy and a 0.396 injection success rate. p50 latency is 32.8 ms on a T4.

### **15. Von (wfzyx)**

[Von](https://huggingface.co/wfzyx/von) is a 395M ModernBERT-large encoder with an option-marker head. It scores all options in one bidirectional pass. It is Apache-2.0 with an 8,192-token context.

The [repo](https://github.com/wfzyx/von) reports 0.096 s p50 on 4 vCPUs and 0.023 s on an A10G. Respan measured Von 1.2 at 0.422 accuracy, the lowest in its table. Its calibration is tuned to JevBench and can mislead out of domain.

### **16. Open-Jev-9B (Zefan Cai)**

[Open-Jev](https://github.com/Zefan-Cai/Open-Jev) ships 2B, 9B and 27B adapters on Qwen3.5 bases. [Open-Jev-9B](https://huggingface.co/ZefanCai/Open-Jev-9B) adds a scalar head and fits one 16 GB GPU. It matches the /v1/systemone request shape but claims no parity.

On a 231-task JevBench subset, the project reports 77.49% for 9B and 85.28% for 27B v1.1. Each candidate is capped at 4,096 tokens. Numeric and timeline tasks are weak.

### **17. OpenJev on DiffusionGemma (razorback16)**

[This OpenJev](https://github.com/razorback16/openjev) reads decisions from NVIDIA’s DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B (4B active). It accepts text plus up to 8 images. It uses the same wire API, so Jev SDKs work unchanged.

The project reports 87.4% on JevBench public and 30 ms p50 at 49 tokens. A free hosted endpoint gives 100M tokens per account. Self-hosting needs an NVIDIA GPU with at least 24 GB.

### **18. InnerJev-4B and InnerJev-27B**

[InnerJev](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03935) comes from a Fudan, Tongji and King’s College London team. It distills LLM reasoning into a single-pass decision. The paper also introduces JEVal: 11,257 instances across 36 datasets.

On JEVal, InnerJev-27B scored 79.24% versus Jev’s 78.38%. Its ECE was 0.0149 against Jev’s 0.0532. InnerJev-4B scored 71.92

articles.content:
Title: The math that OpenAI keeps for itself

URL Source: https://newsletter.danielpaleka.com/p/the-math-that-openai-keeps-for-itself

Published Time: 2026-10-16T08:16:27+00:00

Markdown Content:
OpenAI has recently released more than 700 mathematics results proved by their latest model, bringing human mathematics as we know it to an end. Much ink has been spilled about the impacts of this. Beyond the sheer number of results, what is almost as interesting is what these results _*don’t*_ cover.

The internet commentariat quickly noticed that nothing touched modern cryptography, and some suspected this was no accident:

[ Ben Podgursky@bpodgursky Lucky coincidence the labs are only successfully cracking esoteric math problems and not the problems where a solution would give the winner an asymmetric commerical advantage. 5:46 AM · Oct 7, 2026 · 588K Views 60 Replies · 225 Reposts · 5.62K Likes](https://x.com/bpodgursky/status/2107709224763469984)[ Matthew Green@matthew_d_green @kmad@matthew_pines I think we might lose public key cryptography. 12:31 AM · Oct 8, 2026 · 1.99M Views 250 Replies · 431 Reposts · 5.34K Likes](https://x.com/matthew_d_green/status/2107992246360649879)
But let’s take a look at the data: is cryptography actually underrepresented, and which fields are conspicuously missing from the recent OpenAI math results? This sort of question nowadays is easy to answer with a coding agent and a Semantic Scholar API key. Turns out there are other clear patterns, apart from cryptography.

Precisely, OpenAI has published very few results on statistics, ML theory, optimization, and numerical analysis. These are large parts of mathematics nowadays, making up 20% of arXiv theorems, but less than 1% of the OpenAI results!

One hypothesis is that these fields simply don’t have open problems; but this is not really true. The gap reduces, but is still statistically significant, if we consider only arXiv papers that solve open problems as making up the baseline ratio.

Or could it be that the OpenAI team is just not familiar with open problems in optimization or machine learning theory? Some readers might be familiar with one of the first signs of AI being transformative in math, this tweet in 2025…

[ Sebastien Bubeck@SebastienBubeck Claim: gpt-5-pro can prove new interesting mathematics. Proof: I took a convex optimization paper with a clean open problem in it and asked gpt-5-pro to work on it. It proved a better bound than what is in the paper, and I checked the proof it's correct. Details below.  4:05 PM · Aug 20, 2025 · 7.52M Views 309 Replies · 1.22K Reposts · 8.02K Likes](https://x.com/SebastienBubeck/status/1958198661139009862)
Of course, one explanation is that the portion of math that is missing is the closest to what all labs (not just OpenAI) might want to use internally; hence all labs will generally abstain from publishing, to preserve comparative advantage.

I noticed this discrepancy due to these fields being an old interest of mine. Around 2020, I stopped doing mathematics, largely due to AI. Instead of cutting it completely, I spent about a year and a half not fully letting go, trying to have it both ways. Dabbling in fields such as statistical learning theory, random neural networks, mixed integer optimization, even trying to understand properties of SGD and batch normalization… This was not entirely useless, but to be honest I haven’t used any of it in a while.

Only a single mathematical result in the OpenAI math dump would be professionally interesting to 2020-2021 me: [Max-Cut cannot be approximated better than 0.878 assuming P != NP.](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/A-Direct-Proof-of-Optimal-Max-Cut-Hardness-September-23-2026/paper.pdf) This does not really count, as it falls out as a consequence of a complexity theory result, the excitingly named Unique Games ~~Conjecture~~ Theorem, that OpenAI proved in the same batch.

Back to “math might be useful for LLM training”. My belief is this:

1.   Despite pre-2026 deep learning theory and similar fields being far too weak, asking the wrong questions, and the disconnect to frontier LLMs…

2.   Mathematical capabilities will at some point make a comeback and feed back into LLM training.

The truth of the matter is that mathematics has shown the fastest growth in capability across ~all domains of human expertise. The moment of “math is now solved” we are in now is just a historical blip, as the true ceiling of mathematical ability extends far beyond what people can hope to understand.

Many readers have seen this plot many times; and most have also seen counterarguments. There are bottlenecks—data availability, expensive feedback loops, OOD generalization, etc.—and if we see AIs or AI companies taking over the world, automating everything our civilization does seems like a real grind.

But note that _none of these obstacles apply to mathematics_. You can create synthetic data. Verification is cheap. Curriculum learning is trivial. By now AI for math has been completely derisked, and it is just a matter of adding more compute to get more math. Compute in, math out.

Again, what you should take from noticing AIs have improved in mathematics faster than other fields is not to assume that labs have concentrated immensely on mathematics for some short-term gain. (Human math is, somewhat famously, not economically fruitful.) The correct take is just that **AIs improve in mathematics faster than on other tasks**; if AI labs decide to spend compute, there will be math.

Of course, what’s happening in math, the labs want to make happen in other fields. Recursive self-improvement, widely dismissed as science fiction in polite society about two years ago, is now openly the plan of multiple trillion-dollar companies. The gains in many fields of human activity are coming soon, and they will be dangerous and very unequally distributed.

But whatever the gains in biology or robotics you can get for $1B of compute, the gains in mathematics are, from both a human perspective and just an inherent complexity perspective, much, much, much larger.

What do we do with this information?

For the past decade, if you wanted to help AI go well, trying to prove theorems about deep learning was clearly the wrong move. To be clear, proving theorems is still not worth it. But now is a very good time to start asking questions.

If you’re reading this (possibly because you were a mathematician and now you don’t know what to do) and want to do research,**do not think small**. Read about deep learning, the theory of generalization so far, adversarial examples… and think much bigger. Don’t think Math 2.0; instead, think full Jevons paradox, as conjectured by [Christian Szegedy](https://docs.google.com/document/d/e/2PACX-1vTSh-pyNP3Gi99WMmsinnLmE9V5CDI0HEm6WGbIPMNt3V5SGlClHF8-BetotKHOImrvQDSXmFdiOw8D/pub): “much cheaper and much deeper mathematics will become even more of the fundamental infrastructure of the future.”

I anticipate a future moment when AIs can wield mathematical objects that would take us months to even describe, while being barely superhuman on most other tasks. It would be good to slow down at that point; but if coordination fails, this critical phase before AI eclipses us in everything might only take a few months. It matters so much to have some work done in advance, **in order to have the correct questions lying around at that time** that we can point to, align our intuitions to reality, get something that helps us understand what is going on, and live to see a better future.

Now is the time of research proposals.

Title: Anthropics' Claude cracks a 25-year-old NSA cryptography mystery in under 30 minutes

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-claude-cracks-a-25-year-old-nsa-cryptography-mystery-in-under-30-minutes/

Published Time: 2026-10-17T14:42:56+00:00

Markdown Content:
Oct 17, 2026

**Anthropic's AI Claude has solved a 25-year-old cryptography mystery.** NIST standardized several curves in the ECDSA standard, the most widely used framework for elliptic-curve digital signatures, back in 2000. The NSA had supplied the seeds, the starting values used to generate the curve parameters, with zero explanation. No one knew how they were created, and that fueled suspicion of possible backdoors. The mystery even attracted a [bounty](https://words.filippo.io/seeds-bounty/) and [amateur sleuthing efforts](https://saweis.net/posts/nist-curve-seed-origins.html). The late NSA employee Jerry Solinas had suggested the seeds were a hash of a humorous phrase, but that turned out to be wrong.

Claude cracked it in under 30 minutes. The seeds came from "lrand48," a simple C random number generator, initialized with a Unix timestamp between May 1997 and April 1998. Claude spotted the pattern because "lrand48" only outputs 31 bits, and the top bits in some seeds were systematically zero. According to [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins), this makes deliberate backdoors less likely. Anthropic is donating the $36,864 bounty to the [Internet Security Research Group](https://www.abetterinternet.org/).

Title: Microsoft and CMU Team Up To Train Early Career Software Engineers

URL Source: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/news/2026/microsoft-cmu-praise

Published Time: 2026-10-15T11:00:00-0400

Markdown Content:
In between classes on machine learning and software engineering, Jace Watson isn't heading back to his dorm or finding a quiet place to study somewhere on Carnegie Mellon University's campus.

That's because Watson isn't even in Pittsburgh. He's in Seattle, working at his full-time job as a software engineer at Microsoft and taking classes through the [Preceptorship for AI-accelerated Software Engineering (PRAISE) program](https://commandline.microsoft.com/praise-preceptor-ai-accelerated-software-engineering-cmu/), which CMU and Microsoft launched to train early career software engineers for the rapidly changing computer science landscape.

"When I started undergraduate, it was the beginning of AI being something that everybody had access to on their own computers. As I got closer to graduation, it started becoming clear how big AI tools would be in the workforce, but using AI wasn't a huge part of my education," Watson said. "When I joined Microsoft, these tools were part of my day-to-day, and I wanted to make sure I knew how to fully take advantage of them, which is why I sought out the additional education opportunity through CMU and Microsoft."

CMU and Microsoft launched the Preceptorship for AI-accelerated Software Engineering (PRAISE) program to train early career software engineers for the rapidly changing computer science landscape.

The CMU/Microsoft PRAISE program offers early career Microsoft employees a chance to take online courses in CMU's Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science while receiving hands-on mentorship at the company. At Microsoft, selected early career engineers, or preceptees, work with senior engineering preceptors to build AI-accelerated software engineering skills through structured guidance, mentorship and application to their day-to-day Microsoft work. Participants can also enroll in SCS classes focused on software engineering and artificial intelligence.

"This partnership with Microsoft is about providing the Griffin School of Computer Science's high-quality computer science learning to people who aren't in the traditional education system but are seeking guidance to navigate a rapidly changing landscape," said [SCS Dean Martial Hebert](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/about/about-dean). "SCS and Microsoft recognize that we all have a part to play in supporting and readying the nation's workforce, and the CMU/Microsoft PRAISE program is an innovative step in that direction."

The idea for the program came about following CMU alumnus Mark Russinovich's (ENG 1989, 1994) visit to SCS in October 2025. The chief technology officer, deputy chief information security officer and technical fellow for Microsoft Azure spoke about how AI tools help senior engineers, but noted that the same level of benefit isn't available for junior engineers.

"AI changes the work, but it doesn't eliminate the need for junior engineers or for human judgment and accountability," Russinovich said. "By combining Microsoft's engineering experience with CMU's academic expertise, PRAISE offers a model we're proud to lead and hope others in industry and academia will adopt."

From that discussion, SCS and Microsoft began considering how education could help junior engineers overcome the challenges of using AI in the workplace.

"It used to be that early career software engineers would do a lot of tasks that would build up their expertise," said [Michael Hilton](https://s3d.cmu.edu/people/core-faculty/hilton-michael.html), a teaching professor in CMU's [Software and Societal Systems Department](https://s3d.cmu.edu/index.html) (S3D). "Combining forces between academics and practitioners allows us to bring our expertise together and create solutions that draw on computer science research while standing up to the daily realities of software development."

This semester, Microsoft employees enrolled in the CMU PRAISE certificate program are taking Machine Learning in Production and Preceptorship in AI-Augmented Software Engineering I. These classes train students on how to incorporate machine learning into the software they write and to use AI tools while developing that software.

"That judgment for when to use AI should be viewed as ongoing education, which is why we're partnering with Carnegie Mellon University on curriculum as part of the PRAISE program," Microsoft wrote in their announcement of the partnership. "The intent is to set students up for success in the workplace and accelerate preceptees with formal curricula to complement the guidance from the preceptor on how to build and deliver with confidence."

In the spring semester, students will take DevOps: Engineering for Secure Development and Deployment and the second half of the Preceptorship in AI-Augmented Software Engineering course sequence. These courses can be applied to a master's degree in software engineering, allowing students to further their learning at SCS. CMU hopes to grow the program and add more students to the certificate program, perhaps one day opening the door to other industry partners.

"I am tremendously excited about the impact this program will have on junior engineers at Microsoft," said [Jonathan Aldrich](https://s3d.cmu.edu/people/core-faculty/aldrich-jonathan.html), an S3D professor who directs the PRAISE certificate program. "With so many companies worldwide faced with upheaval due to AI in software development, I believe this program will become a template for rapidly leveling up new developers across the industry."

To learn more about the program, [visit Microsoft's Command Line](https://commandline.microsoft.com/praise-preceptor-ai-accelerated-software-engineering-cmu/).

Title: Pattern Matching Beats Narrative Reasoning

URL Source: https://blog.scottstevenson.net/p/pattern-matching-beats-narrative

Published Time: 2024-08-14T09:30:40+00:00

Markdown Content:
Most of my losing bets, in both business and investing, were driven by _narrative_ _reasoning: s_ hort compelling stories about the world that sound smart.

“Marijuana is about to be legalized in Canada. This is a rare opportunity to invest at the ground floor of a new industry.”

“I’m going to invest in a cobalt mining company because they won a contract with Tesla.”

Before we launched [Spellbook](http://spellbook.legal/), we thought: “Let’s launch Shopify for Lawyers, because hourly billing lawyers care more about getting business than efficiency”

We love stories. Narratives are like a virus and a mind-altering drug. When they hit our ears we feel: “Ah! That makes sense”. They add clarity in an overwhelming world. And then we feel compelled to share the story with others. The clarity felt good and we want to share that feeling. More importantly, sharing the story makes us feel smart.

This contagiousness makes narrative reasoning extremely dangerous. Because simple stories often make horrible bets.

Concise stories don’t work well to drive action in the real world, because the real world is so _multi-causal._ There are hundreds, or even millions of factors that cause a bet to have a good outcome.

Imagine the best chess AI engine in the world: for any board state, it has to consider hundreds moves, and then a huge number of branching futures. Great chess engines can’t simply use narrative reasoning like: “a good offense is the best defense” to win. These engines are more like spreadsheets: massive matrices of numbers and probabilities. They can make moves that are impossible for us to comprehend using language-based reasoning.

The worst part? Real life is _way_ more complex than chess.

From this we can conclude that the _most optimal_ way of strategizing about the world is definitely not by using a short sequence of words.

Raw reality is not very _legible_. That is, it’s not simply structured and easily comprehensible by us. Although narratives make us comfortable, they’re not enough to capture the essence of reality. Reality is messy.

One of the most impactful things I’ve ever read is Venkatesh Rao’s “[A Big Little Idea Called Legibility](https://www.ribbonfarm.com/2010/07/26/a-big-little-idea-called-legibility/)”. It talks about how we are drawn to orderly, legible systems—but how those systems often fail. We even tear up messy, working systems, replace them with nice orderly systems, and see the order fail terribly. We put too much value on legibility. Let’s call this _legibility bias._

For instance, in the image below there is a legible “scientific forest” and an illegible organic forest. “Scientific forests” were a failure, even though their legible structure made us feel confident in the approach. Messy illegible forests remain successful.

Why does legibility bias persist across society, even when we are aware of it? One answer is: it soothes people. We are conditioned from kindergarten onwards to believe that there is a crisp, clear structure to the world. That there are crisp _reasons why things happen._ In the world of startups, that illusion is demolished if you stick at it long enough. But large organizations “cast the illusion” of legibility to soothe and create a sense of order among employees, while those in the inner circle of upper management face messy reality head-on.

Also in organizations, communication bandwidth means that you need crude, simple stories to get the ship headed in the right direction. Simple stories are a necessary evil in management. But big decisions at the top of an organization are not _actually_ being made this way. Simple stories are a tool to motivate and direct people in approximately the right direction.

If someone has spent years at a large company, and has not been in the “inner circle” of management—it is easy to see how they might confuse the tool that is being used to motivate them with the process in which effective decisions are actually being made.

People misunderstand the utility of simple stories. They’re more of a management tool, a political tool, a motivation tool, and a marketing tool than a _decision making tool_.

Good bet making is about “finding alpha”. That is, betting on opportunities that others have underestimated. Since humans have a strong _**bias for legibility**_, highly legible bets get bandwagoned.

For example: “Since marijuana just got legalized in Canada, I’m going to buy $WEED stock to get in at the ground floor of a new industry”

Here’s how that worked out:

Even if these narratives _are_ correct, they are too visible to markets and get quickly over-bought. In other words: The stock price gets too high before you make your bet. Or too many competitors get to the business idea before you. Or too many musicians make similar sounding songs. This reasoning works across any competitive domain.

A really good place to find bets that are underestimated is in the illegible.

If stories don’t work, how do we survive at all in a world so complex and multi-causal? Well, simple stories can work for basic survival: “I need to eat to survive”.

But to find good bets that others don’t see, we need to leave crisp stories behind and think more like a chess engine. We need to digest raw hyper-dimensional reality. But how do we do that without putting our situation into a 100,000 x 100,000 spreadsheet?

The first answer is: _intuition_.

We already have 86 billion neurons in our brain that are doing something similar to a chess engine. We can’t see exactly how it works, but it can send us much more valuable signals about the world than narratives do. If we digest enough data, our brain starts pattern matching automatically. Pattern matching is how we position ourselves to throw a basketball and recognize our friends faces. Those are not things we think about in words.

Our brains are really good at pattern matching without using words.

Running fast using intuition to make decisions can be extraordinarily effective.

But what if our intuition is bad? What if our intuition differs from that of our team?

That’s a lot of words to say: “trust your gut!”. But what if you haven’t developed intuition? Or what if your intuition disagrees with the intuition of your team?

There is a slightly more legible approach that I’ve found effective:

Look at your past bets and ask yourself: what are the 10-20 attributes that mattered? List them out, and then go through each of your winning and losing bets, noticing which attributes they had.

We did this for all the product feature bets we made at Spellbook, and were able to correlate 16 attributes with what made a successful product bet. And many were surprising.

Almost none of our correlated attributes had to do with the narrative of the feature itself. We discovered a bunch of other things that mattered:

*   Can a lawyer get value from the feature instantly with absolutely zero configuration?

*   Was someone on the team so inspired to build something that they “started without permission”?

*   Is the feature “whole” rather than a stepping stone to get somewhere else?

*   Can the feature be fully prototyped in 2 weeks?

We ended up with a framework that is a middle ground between legible, narrative based reasoning and intuition. And the best part is we could objectively score prospective bets in this framework.

It brings us a little closer to reasoning like a chess engine. These signals increased our hit rate significantly when we used to not hit at all.

For years we had been listening to the gospel: “talk to your customers! Build what they ask for!” This was helpful, but it had an catastrophic blindspot that was causing us to make losing bets for years.

We were missing an entire universe of patterns outside of the tunnel vision of stories.

This approach also helped dramatically improve my performance in investing.

When I started noodling in active investing almost 20 years ago, I relied on narrative “reasons” and news headlines to make bets. My active portfolio produced neutral returns for nearly 10 years (adjusted for inflation, that’s a big loss). Those narratives simply didn’t capture the thousands of factors that impacted stock price. And if they did: well everyone else was jumping on the same bandwagon and pushing up the buy price where the bet became too expensive to make sense.

Over the last 9 years I switched to a pattern matching approach. My active portfolio has performed ~20x better than my passive portfolio over that period.

To improve my ability to pattern match, I really like to “soak” in data. I read lots of charts and try to make written predictions on them regularly. I check back on how my predictions fared. Eventually making trades started to feel like throwing a basketball. My brain started to develop a deep intuition for technical and fundamental signals, and how they combine to make a “swish”.

Pattern matching is not hard. Our brains are wired to do it. The hard part is being independent-minded enough to believe your own conclusions.

To do that, you need to escape the universe of simple stories we are surrounded by. Stories are the threads that hold society together. We are fish and stories are our water. Repeating popular stories grants us head nods and social acceptance.

For example, “You can’t beat the market, dollar-cost average into index funds!” is the kind of viral story that will earn you nods of approval from millennials and upvotes on Reddit.

Pattern matching, on the other hand, can drive you to make moves like an advanced chess engine. Moves that others find alien and incomprehensible.

If your bets don’t generate some confused looks, they’re probably too obvious, and thus overdone.

> “To believe that what is true for you in your private heart, is true for all men,—that is genius” —Ralph Waldo Emerson, [Self-Reliance](https://archive.vcu.edu/english/engweb/transcendentalism/authors/emerson/essays/selfreliance.html)
